os-concurrency:0.prompt: What do two threads of the same process share that two separate processes do not?
options: Their call stacks, so they can call each other's functions
The heap, globals and open file descriptors
Their saved CPU registers and program counter
Their thread ids
os-concurrency:0.explanation: Threads in one process share memory and resources, which makes communication cheap but races possible. Each thread still has its own stack and registers; separate processes get separate address spaces and must use IPC.

os-concurrency:0.prompt: A Node.js API hashes passwords with a pure-JavaScript CPU-heavy function inside an async handler. Under load, all requests slow down. Why?
options: async functions are scheduled onto libuv's thread pool automatically
async/await doesn't move CPU work off the event loop
Promises are slower than callbacks
The handler should use a callback instead of returning a promise
os-concurrency:0.explanation: Marking a function async doesn't move work off the main thread; it only lets it pause at awaits. CPU-bound work needs worker_threads, a child process, or a native async API (e.g. crypto.scrypt, which uses the libuv pool).

os-concurrency:0.prompt: Which is the key difference between a coroutine (or an async function) and an OS thread?
options: Coroutines are scheduled by the kernel, threads by the language runtime
Coroutines yield only at defined points; threads can be preempted
Threads can't share memory
Coroutines always run in parallel across multiple cores
os-concurrency:0.explanation: Coroutines are cooperatively scheduled: they switch only where they yield (e.g. await), so code between yields runs atomically relative to other coroutines on that thread. Kernel threads are preemptive and, on multicore, truly parallel.

os-concurrency:0.prompt: You need to run an untrusted image-processing library that may crash or leak memory, from a Node server. Which isolation is the safest choice?
options: Run it in the same thread inside try/catch
Run it in a worker_thread
Run it in a separate child process
Wrap it in an async function
os-concurrency:0.explanation: A separate process has its own address space, so a native crash or leak can't take down the server and the OS reclaims memory when it exits. worker_threads share the process, so a native segfault still kills everything; try/catch can't catch a segfault.

os-concurrency:0.prompt: When is moving work to worker_threads in Node.js the right call?
options: For network-bound calls to a database that take several hundred ms
For CPU-bound JavaScript like parsing or resizing in JS
For reading files, since fs is synchronous
Whenever a route's average latency is above 100 ms
os-concurrency:0.explanation: Workers give parallel JS execution for CPU-heavy tasks. I/O-bound work is already non-blocking via libuv, so workers add overhead without benefit; slowness from waiting on a DB isn't fixed by more threads.

os-concurrency:0.prompt: A Go service handles 100k concurrent connections with one goroutine each, while a Java service with one platform thread per connection struggles at 10k. What explains the difference?
options: Go compiles to faster machine code than the JVM's JIT can produce
Goroutines are cheap runtime-scheduled tasks on few OS threads
Java can't open more than 10k sockets
Go uses UDP by default for its HTTP server
os-concurrency:0.explanation: Goroutines start with a few KB of stack and are scheduled by the Go runtime, so 100k of them is cheap. Platform threads typically reserve around 1 MB of stack each and are kernel-scheduled. Java 21 virtual threads close this gap the same way.

Each async function runs synchronously until its first await, then yields. So a1, b1 and main print first; the continuations a2 and b2 run later as microtasks in order. This is coroutine-style interleaving on a single thread.

A 0 ms timer can't preempt running JS: the busy loop holds the only JS thread for 50 ms, so 'loop done' prints first and the timer fires late (elapsed >= 50). Single-threaded event loops have no preemption.

os-concurrency:0.prompt: Which statements about processes vs threads are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Creating a thread is usually cheaper than creating a process
A crash (e.g. segfault) in one thread usually kills the whole process
Threads in the same process need IPC like pipes to share data
Separate processes give stronger fault and memory isolation
Threads of one process each get their own heap
os-concurrency:0.explanation: Threads share the address space, so they're cheap to create and share data directly, but one fatal fault kills all of them. Processes isolate memory and faults at higher cost. Threads share one heap and don't need IPC.

os-concurrency:0.prompt: In Node.js, which of these run work outside the main JavaScript thread? Select all that apply.
options: fs.readFile (via the libuv thread pool)
crypto.pbkdf2 with a callback
A for-loop inside an async function
worker_threads Worker
JSON.parse of a large string
os-concurrency:0.explanation: Async fs and crypto functions offload to libuv's thread pool, and Workers are separate threads with their own V8 isolate. A for-loop and JSON.parse run synchronously on the main thread, even inside an async function.

os-concurrency:0.prompt: Two JavaScript async functions running in the same Node.js thread can be interrupted mid-statement by each other, just like preemptive threads.
options: True
False
os-concurrency:0.explanation: False. JS on one thread runs to completion between await points; another async function only runs when the current one yields. Races still happen, but only across awaits, not in the middle of a synchronous statement.

os-concurrency:1.prompt: What does the kernel save and restore during a context switch between threads?
options: The entire heap of the process, copied to a per-thread save area
Registers, program counter and stack pointer
Only the open file descriptors
The thread's local variables, copied from its stack into the kernel
os-concurrency:1.explanation: A context switch saves the outgoing thread's CPU state (registers, PC, SP, flags) and loads the next one's. For switches across processes, the memory mapping (page tables) changes too; the heap itself is never copied.

os-concurrency:1.prompt: What usually triggers an involuntary (preemptive) context switch?
options: The thread calls read() on a socket that has no data yet
Its time slice ends or a higher-priority task wakes
The thread calls sleep()
The thread waits on a mutex held by another thread
os-concurrency:1.explanation: Involuntary switches happen when the scheduler takes the CPU away (time slice expired or preemption by a more urgent task). Blocking on I/O, sleeping or waiting on a lock are voluntary switches: the thread gives up the CPU itself.

os-concurrency:1.prompt: A service runs 2,000 busy OS threads on an 8-core machine and throughput drops as threads are added. What's the most likely cause?
options: The kernel caps each process at 8 runnable threads
Constant switching and cache thrashing
Too few threads for the cores
Threads of one process can't run on more than one core at a time
os-concurrency:1.explanation: With far more runnable threads than cores, the scheduler switches constantly and each switch evicts useful cache lines. For CPU-bound work a pool sized near the core count is usually best; there's no 8-thread limit.

os-concurrency:1.prompt: Which is the main reason a context switch between processes tends to cost more than one between threads of the same process?
options: Processes have more registers to save
Page tables change, so TLB entries go cold
Threads don't use the CPU cache, so there's nothing to invalidate
Processes must be swapped out to disk before another can run
os-concurrency:1.explanation: Switching processes changes the memory mapping, which costs page-table switches and TLB misses afterwards (partly mitigated by PCID/ASID tags). Same-process threads keep the mapping. Swapping to disk isn't part of a normal switch.

options: Threads run until they voluntarily yield or block
The OS can forcibly take the CPU from a thread
Threads are dispatched in strict priority order and never interrupted
Only one process exists at a time
os-concurrency:1.explanation: Preemption lets the kernel interrupt a running thread so one misbehaving thread can't monopolise the CPU. Cooperative scheduling, where tasks run until they yield, is how JS event loops and coroutines work.

os-concurrency:1.prompt: A Node.js container is limited to 0.5 CPU via a cgroup CPU quota, and p99 latency shows periodic 50–100 ms spikes even at modest load. What's a likely cause?
options: DNS lookups are cached and expire every 100 ms
CFS quota throttling pauses the container each period
The event loop has too many microtasks queued
TCP Nagle's algorithm
os-concurrency:1.explanation: With a quota of 50 ms per 100 ms period, bursts (including GC and libuv threads) can use the quota early, then the cgroup is throttled for the rest of the period. Check nr_throttled in cpu.stat; raise the limit or smooth work.

os-concurrency:1.prompt: Why do latency-sensitive systems sometimes pin threads to specific CPU cores (CPU affinity)?
options: Pinning raises the core's clock speed
It keeps caches warm and avoids migrations
It disables context switching entirely on that core for the pinned thread
It's required to use more than one core
os-concurrency:1.explanation: Migrating a thread between cores loses warm L1/L2 caches; pinning (taskset, sched_setaffinity) keeps locality and predictable latency. Interrupts and other tasks can still preempt the thread unless the core is isolated.

os-concurrency:1.prompt: Which events cause a thread to give up the CPU voluntarily? Select all that apply.
options: Calling a blocking read() on a socket with no data
Waiting on a contended mutex
Its time slice expiring
Calling sleep() or nanosleep()
A higher-priority thread becoming runnable
os-concurrency:1.explanation: Blocking I/O, waiting on locks and sleeping are voluntary: the thread asks to wait. Time-slice expiry and being preempted by a higher-priority thread are involuntary switches imposed by the scheduler.

os-concurrency:1.prompt: Which tools or metrics help diagnose excessive context switching on Linux? Select all that apply.
options: The `cs` column in `vmstat 1`
`pidstat -w` per-task voluntary and non-voluntary switch rates
`voluntary_ctxt_switches` in /proc/<pid>/status
`df -h`
`ls -la /proc`
os-concurrency:1.explanation: vmstat shows system-wide switch rates, pidstat -w and /proc/<pid>/status break them down per task into voluntary (blocking) and involuntary (preempted). df reports disk usage; listing /proc shows nothing about switch rates.

os-concurrency:1.prompt: A high rate of involuntary context switches for a process suggests it is CPU-bound and competing with other runnable tasks for cores.
options: True
False
os-concurrency:1.explanation: True. Involuntary switches mean the scheduler preempted the task while it still wanted to run. Lots of voluntary switches instead point to blocking on I/O or locks.

os-concurrency:1.prompt: Making a time slice (quantum) extremely short always improves overall system throughput because every task gets the CPU sooner.
options: True
False
os-concurrency:1.explanation: False. Very short slices improve responsiveness but increase the fraction of time spent switching and hurt cache locality, so throughput drops. Schedulers balance latency against switching overhead.

os-concurrency:2.prompt: You need to allow at most 10 concurrent connections to a downstream service from a thread pool of 50. Which primitive fits best?
options: A mutex
A counting semaphore initialised to 10
A condition variable alone
A spinlock
os-concurrency:2.explanation: A counting semaphore tracks N available permits: acquire decrements, release increments, and callers block at zero. A mutex only allows one holder; a condition variable needs a mutex and a predicate to express the same thing.

os-concurrency:2.prompt: What is the key semantic difference between a mutex and a binary semaphore?
options: A semaphore can only be shared between processes, never threads
A mutex has an owner; a semaphore doesn't
A mutex allows two holders at once
There is no difference; the names are interchangeable in POSIX
os-concurrency:2.explanation: Ownership lets mutexes support priority inheritance, recursive locking and error checking. Semaphores are signalling counters, so one thread can post and another wait, which makes them useful for producer/consumer handoffs but not for ownership-based protection.

os-concurrency:2.prompt: Why must a thread wait on a condition variable inside a `while (!condition)` loop rather than an `if`?
options: A while loop is faster than an if, because the compiler can unroll it
Wakeups can be spurious or the state may change
Condition variables require loops by syntax
It prevents the mutex from being released while the thread sleeps
os-concurrency:2.explanation: Waking up doesn't guarantee the predicate still holds: wakeups can be spurious, and with notify_all another consumer may grab the item first. Re-checking in a loop after reacquiring the mutex is the correct pattern.

os-concurrency:2.prompt: What does `pthread_cond_wait(&cv, &mutex)` do with the mutex?
options: Nothing; you must unlock it manually before calling wait
Releases it atomically, then reacquires it on wake
Destroys the mutex
Locks it a second time so the waiting thread keeps exclusive access
os-concurrency:2.explanation: The atomic unlock-and-sleep is what prevents a lost wakeup between checking the condition and starting to wait. On return the thread holds the mutex again so it can safely re-check the predicate.

os-concurrency:2.prompt: Threads hold a lock for about 50 ns at a time on a multicore machine. Which lock type might be preferable, and why?
options: A sleeping mutex, because spinning is always wasteful
A spinlock: spinning beats a context switch here
A semaphore with count 0
No lock at all, because a 50 ns window is too short for two threads to collide
os-concurrency:2.explanation: When the expected wait is shorter than a context switch (microseconds), spinning wins. Spinlocks are bad for long holds or single-core systems, which is why adaptive mutexes spin briefly and then sleep. Short critical sections still race without a lock.

os-concurrency:2.prompt: In a bounded producer/consumer queue using one mutex and two condition variables (notFull, notEmpty), what should the producer do after inserting an item?
options: Signal notFull, since the producer just used a slot
Signal notEmpty to wake a consumer
Destroy the mutex
Busy-wait until the queue is empty again
os-concurrency:2.explanation: The producer just made the queue non-empty, so it wakes a consumer waiting on notEmpty. Consumers signal notFull after removing an item. Signalling the wrong condition variable leaves waiters asleep.

os-concurrency:2.prompt: A read-heavy cache (99% reads) is protected by a single mutex and shows lock contention. Which change helps most while staying correct?
options: Remove the lock, since reads alone can't corrupt the data structure
Use a reader-writer lock
Use a semaphore with count 0
Add sleep() calls in readers
os-concurrency:2.explanation: Reader-writer locks allow parallel readers and exclusive writers, which suits read-heavy data. Watch for writer starvation with reader-preferring implementations. Removing the lock causes data races.

os-concurrency:2.prompt: Which statements about synchronisation primitives are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A counting semaphore can limit concurrency to N
Condition variables are always used together with a mutex
A spinlock puts the waiting thread to sleep immediately
Recursive mutexes let the owning thread lock the same mutex multiple times
A binary semaphore enforces that only the acquiring thread can release it
os-concurrency:2.explanation: Semaphores count permits, condition variables pair with a mutex that protects the predicate, and recursive mutexes track a lock count per owner. Spinlocks busy-wait instead of sleeping, and semaphores have no ownership.

os-concurrency:2.prompt: You want to limit a Node.js service to 5 concurrent outbound requests to a rate-limited API. Which approaches implement semaphore-like behaviour? Select all that apply.
options: A counter plus a queue of pending resolvers: acquire awaits when the counter hits 5, release resolves the next waiter
A library such as p-limit with concurrency 5
Wrapping each call in setTimeout(fn, 0)
An undici/http Agent with a maximum of 5 connections to that host
Using Promise.all on all requests at once
os-concurrency:2.explanation: A counter with a waiter queue is a semaphore; p-limit packages that, and an agent's connection cap limits concurrency at the socket level. setTimeout just delays, and Promise.all fires everything at once.

os-concurrency:2.prompt: Calling signal (notify_one) on a condition variable when no thread is waiting has no lasting effect: the signal is not remembered for a future waiter.
options: True
False
os-concurrency:2.explanation: True. Condition variables are stateless; a signal with no waiters is lost. That's why waiters must check a shared predicate under the mutex before waiting. Semaphores, by contrast, remember posts in their count.

os-concurrency:2.prompt: Because Node.js runs JavaScript on a single thread, you never need mutex-like coordination in Node application code.
options: True
False
os-concurrency:2.explanation: False. Interleaving across awaits causes logical races (check-then-act on shared state or a database), and worker_threads sharing a SharedArrayBuffer need Atomics. Async mutexes and DB locks are still common in Node.

os-concurrency:3.prompt: Thread 1 locks A then B; thread 2 locks B then A. Occasionally both hang forever. Which fix removes the deadlock most directly?
options: Add a short sleep between acquiring the first and second lock
Acquire locks in one global order
Use more threads
Increase the CPU count
os-concurrency:3.explanation: A consistent lock order makes a circular wait impossible, breaking one of the four Coffman conditions. Sleeps only change timing (the bug becomes rarer, not gone), and more threads or CPUs don't affect the cycle.

os-concurrency:3.prompt: Using tryLock with a timeout, and releasing held locks on failure before retrying, prevents deadlock by breaking which condition?
options: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
Circular wait only by ordering
Bounded waiting
os-concurrency:3.explanation: When a thread gives up the locks it holds after failing to get the next one, it never holds while waiting indefinitely. Mutual exclusion still applies, and no ordering is imposed. 'Bounded waiting' isn't a Coffman condition.

os-concurrency:3.prompt: Two threads keep detecting a conflict, both back off, and both retry at the same moment, forever. Neither is blocked, but no progress is made. What is this called?
options: Deadlock
Livelock
Starvation
Priority inversion
os-concurrency:3.explanation: Livelock: threads are active and responding to each other but make no progress. In a deadlock they're blocked waiting. Randomised (jittered) backoff is the usual fix.

os-concurrency:3.prompt: In PostgreSQL, two transactions update the same two rows in opposite order and deadlock. What does PostgreSQL do?
options: Both wait forever until an admin kills one of the sessions
It detects the cycle and aborts one transaction
It silently merges both updates
It escalates both row locks to a table lock and serialises the transactions
os-concurrency:3.explanation: PostgreSQL detects lock cycles (checking after deadlock_timeout, 1s by default) and cancels one transaction with SQLSTATE 40P01. The application should retry it; updating rows in a consistent order (e.g. by id) prevents it.

os-concurrency:3.prompt: What is the difference between deadlock prevention and deadlock avoidance?
options: They're the same thing
Prevention removes a condition by design; avoidance grants requests only if safe
Avoidance means killing processes after a deadlock happens
Prevention only applies to databases, avoidance to OS kernels and threads
os-concurrency:3.explanation: Prevention designs deadlock out; avoidance needs advance knowledge of maximum resource needs and decides dynamically. Detection-and-recovery (what databases do) is a third strategy: let it happen, find the cycle, abort a victim.

os-concurrency:3.prompt: A transfer function locks `from` then `to` account mutexes. transfer(A, B) and transfer(B, A) run concurrently and deadlock. What's the most robust fix?
options: Lock the smaller account id first
Lock `to` before `from` in every transfer, regardless of direction
Use one global lock
Retry the transfer after a short random sleep whenever it takes too long
os-concurrency:3.explanation: Ordering by a stable key (id) gives a global order no matter which direction the transfer goes. Swapping to 'to before from' still deadlocks for opposite transfers. A global lock is correct but kills concurrency.

os-concurrency:3.prompt: In a wait-for graph with single-instance resources, what indicates a deadlock?
options: Any node with more than two edges
A cycle in the graph
A node with no outgoing edges
The graph being disconnected
os-concurrency:3.explanation: With one instance per resource, a cycle in the wait-for graph means every thread in it waits on another in the cycle: deadlock. With multiple instances per resource, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient.

os-concurrency:3.prompt: Which practices reduce deadlock risk in application code? Select all that apply.
options: Acquire locks in a documented global order
Hold locks for as short a time as possible and never across network calls
Use lock timeouts and handle the failure
Call unknown callbacks while holding a lock
Nest as many locks as needed for convenience
os-concurrency:3.explanation: Ordering, short critical sections and timeouts all shrink the window or break a Coffman condition. Calling foreign code under a lock can acquire other locks in unknown order, and deep nesting multiplies ordering hazards.

os-concurrency:3.prompt: Two Node.js services each hold a Redis lock and wait for the other's lock with no TTL. Which measures prevent a permanent hang? Select all that apply.
options: Give every lock a TTL so it expires if the holder stalls or dies
Acquire both locks in a consistent order (e.g. sorted key names)
Acquire with a bounded wait and release what you hold on failure
Store locks in a JavaScript Map instead of Redis
Retry immediately in a tight loop forever
os-concurrency:3.explanation: TTLs bound how long a stuck lock can block, ordering removes the cycle, and bounded waits break hold-and-wait. An in-process Map doesn't coordinate across services, and tight retries just burn CPU.

os-concurrency:3.prompt: If a system eliminates any one of the four Coffman conditions, resource deadlock cannot occur.
options: True
False
os-concurrency:3.explanation: True. Deadlock requires mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait all at once. Breaking any one, most practically circular wait through lock ordering, prevents it.

os-concurrency:3.prompt: Deadlock and starvation are the same problem: in both, a set of threads is permanently blocked waiting on each other.
options: True
False
os-concurrency:3.explanation: False. In deadlock, threads wait on each other in a cycle and nobody progresses. In starvation, the system makes progress but some thread is repeatedly passed over (e.g. low priority, unfair locks).

os-concurrency:4.explanation: Both calls run their check synchronously before either reaches the await, so both see balance 100 and both subtract: ok,ok and -60. The await between the check and the write is the race window, even on one thread.
All three read count = 0 before any await resumes, then each writes 0 + 1. That's a lost update: the result is 1. Doing the read and write in the same synchronous step (count++) avoids it.

Chaining each operation onto the previous promise serialises them like a mutex: the second check runs only after the first finishes, sees 20 and is denied. The `.catch` keeps one failure from breaking the chain.

os-concurrency:4.prompt: A Node signup handler does `if (!(await db.users.findOne({ email }))) await db.users.insertOne({ email })`. Duplicate accounts appear under load. What's the most robust fix?
options: Wrap both calls in try/catch
Add a unique index on email
Add `await sleep(10)` before the insert to let earlier requests finish
Run Node with a single cluster worker so requests can't overlap
os-concurrency:4.explanation: The check and the insert are separate round trips, so two requests can both pass the check. A unique index makes the database enforce it atomically. A single Node process still interleaves at awaits, and sleeps only shift timing.

os-concurrency:4.prompt: A cache helper does `if (!cache.has(k)) cache.set(k, await fetchUser(k))`. 100 concurrent requests for the same cold key arrive. What happens?
options: fetchUser runs once; the other requests wait on it automatically
fetchUser runs up to 100 times
Node throws a concurrency error
The Map deduplicates the set calls, so only one fetch is issued
os-concurrency:4.explanation: Each request checks the cache before any fetch resolves, so all miss: a cache stampede. Storing the in-flight promise (cache.set(k, promise)) synchronously before awaiting makes later callers share the same fetch.

os-concurrency:4.prompt: Which version of 'decrement stock if available' is safe against concurrent requests in MongoDB?
options: findOne the product, check stock > 0 in JS, then updateOne with $inc: -1
updateOne({ _id, stock: { $gt: 0 } }, { $inc: { stock: -1 } }) and check modifiedCount
Read stock, sleep 10 ms, re-read, then write
Use a global JavaScript boolean flag as a lock
os-concurrency:4.explanation: A conditional update makes the check and the write one atomic operation on the server; modifiedCount 0 means out of stock. Read-then-write in JS has a race window, and a JS flag doesn't cover other processes.

os-concurrency:4.prompt: Your Node app runs 4 instances behind a load balancer. An in-memory async mutex protects a 'generate monthly invoice' job, yet invoices are duplicated. Why?
options: Async mutexes don't work in Node
In-memory locks don't span processes
The load balancer is retrying the job requests after timeouts
Promises from different instances resolve out of order
os-concurrency:4.explanation: In-memory locks are per process. Cross-instance correctness needs shared state: a unique (customer, month) constraint, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or a lease-based distributed lock. LB retries could add duplicates but don't explain the design flaw.

os-concurrency:4.prompt: Which patterns are vulnerable to check-then-act races in async Node.js code? Select all that apply.
options: Read a row, await something, then write based on the stale read
if (!exists) await create() without a unique constraint
A single atomic UPDATE ... WHERE condition statement
Checking a file exists with fs.promises.access, then opening it
Incrementing a local variable inside a synchronous loop
os-concurrency:4.explanation: Any gap between a check and its dependent action lets another task change the state; the fs access-then-open pattern is a classic TOCTOU bug (open directly and handle the error instead). Atomic conditional updates and purely synchronous code have no gap.

os-concurrency:4.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which techniques prevent two concurrent requests from both reserving the last seat? Select all that apply.
options: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the seat row inside a transaction before updating it
UPDATE seats SET held_by = $1 WHERE id = $2 AND held_by IS NULL, then check the row count
Optimistic locking with a version column, retrying on a 0-row update
Reading the seat at READ COMMITTED and updating it in a later, separate transaction
Caching seat availability in each Node process
os-concurrency:4.explanation: Row locks, conditional updates and optimistic version checks all make the decision atomic with the write. A read in one transaction and a write in another leaves a race, and per-process caches can't coordinate instances.

os-concurrency:4.prompt: Code between two `await`s in the same async function runs without interruption from other JavaScript on the same thread.
options: True
False
os-concurrency:4.explanation: True. JS runs to completion between yields, so a synchronous block is effectively atomic relative to other tasks on that thread. Races arise only when shared state is read before an await and used after it.

os-concurrency:4.prompt: Wrapping a check-then-act sequence in a MongoDB or PostgreSQL transaction always makes it safe, regardless of isolation level.
options: True
False
os-concurrency:4.explanation: False. At PostgreSQL's default READ COMMITTED, two transactions can both read 'available' and both insert. You still need row locks, unique constraints, conditional updates or SERIALIZABLE (with retries) to close the race.

os-concurrency:5.prompt: Why does a single-threaded Node.js server handle 10,000 idle WebSocket connections without 10,000 threads?
options: Node creates one hidden libuv thread per open socket
One thread waits on epoll/kqueue for ready sockets
WebSockets don't use TCP
V8 compiles each socket handler into machine code that runs in the kernel
os-concurrency:5.explanation: Readiness notification lets one thread multiplex many sockets: idle connections cost only kernel bookkeeping and a little memory, no thread or stack each. No hidden per-socket threads exist for network I/O.

os-concurrency:5.prompt: Why do select() and poll() scale worse than epoll for many mostly idle connections?
options: They only work with UDP
Every call scans all watched descriptors
They can't watch more than one socket per call, so you need one thread each
They require root privileges
os-concurrency:5.explanation: select/poll are O(n) per call in watched descriptors (and select has an FD_SETSIZE limit, typically 1024). epoll keeps the interest set in the kernel and returns only ready descriptors.

os-concurrency:5.prompt: Which OS mechanism does libuv use for network I/O on macOS?
options: epoll
kqueue
IOCP
io_uring
os-concurrency:5.explanation: libuv uses epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS and the BSDs, and IOCP (completion ports) on Windows. io_uring is a newer Linux interface, not used on macOS.

os-concurrency:5.prompt: A Node service does heavy fs.readFile and crypto.pbkdf2 work, and calls queue up even though CPU is low. Which setting is most likely to help?
options: Increase --max-old-space-size so more requests fit in memory
Increase UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE (default 4)
Use more epoll instances
Increase the TCP listen backlog so fewer calls are rejected
os-concurrency:5.explanation: File system ops, pbkdf2/scrypt and dns.lookup run on libuv's thread pool, which has 4 threads by default, so a fifth task waits. Heap size and the TCP backlog don't affect thread-pool queueing.

os-concurrency:5.prompt: Why does libuv use a thread pool for regular file reads instead of epoll?
options: Files are too large for epoll's buffers
Files always look 'ready' yet reads can block on disk
epoll is only for UDP
File reads are CPU-bound, so they need real threads to run in parallel
os-concurrency:5.explanation: epoll doesn't support regular files in a useful way (they're always considered readable), yet a read may block waiting on disk. libuv therefore does blocking file I/O on pool threads. Sockets and pipes work with epoll.

os-concurrency:5.prompt: In edge-triggered epoll mode (EPOLLET), what must a handler do when notified that a socket is readable?
options: Read one byte and return
Read until EAGAIN
Close the socket and reopen it after processing
Call epoll_ctl to re-add the descriptor after every event
os-concurrency:5.explanation: Edge-triggered mode notifies on state changes only, so leftover unread data won't trigger another event and the connection can stall. Level-triggered (the default) keeps reporting while data remains, which is more forgiving.

os-concurrency:5.prompt: A Node server stops accepting new connections and logs 'EMFILE: too many open files' at about 1,024 sockets. What's the likely fix?
options: Switch from epoll to select
Raise the fd limit and fix leaked sockets
Increase UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE so more sockets can be handled
Add more RAM to the container so the kernel allows more sockets
os-concurrency:5.explanation: Every socket is a file descriptor, and many systems default to a soft limit of 1,024. Raise the limit and check for leaks (e.g. sockets never closed). select would be worse; the thread pool is unrelated.

os-concurrency:5.prompt: In Node.js, which operations use the libuv thread pool rather than OS readiness notification? Select all that apply.
options: fs.promises.readFile
Incoming HTTP requests on a TCP socket
dns.lookup (used by default when connecting to a hostname)
crypto.scrypt with a callback
Reading from a WebSocket
os-concurrency:5.explanation: File I/O, dns.lookup (it wraps getaddrinfo, which blocks) and async crypto use the pool. TCP sockets, including HTTP and WebSockets, use epoll/kqueue on the loop thread. dns.resolve uses c-ares over the network instead.

os-concurrency:5.prompt: Which statements about why Node scales I/O well are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Idle connections cost memory for buffers but no dedicated thread
Throughput depends on keeping each callback short so the loop can service other ready sockets
Node parallelises CPU-bound JavaScript across all cores automatically
One slow synchronous operation delays every connection on that process
epoll eliminates the need for any user-space buffering
os-concurrency:5.explanation: The event-loop model is cheap per connection but relies on short, non-blocking callbacks; one blocking call stalls everything. Node doesn't spread JS across cores (use cluster or workers), and buffers are still needed.

os-concurrency:5.prompt: epoll in its default level-triggered mode keeps reporting a socket as readable on each epoll_wait call as long as unread data remains.
options: True
False
os-concurrency:5.explanation: True. Level-triggered means 'is it ready now?', so unread data keeps producing events. Edge-triggered reports only transitions, which is why it requires draining until EAGAIN.

os-concurrency:5.prompt: Because Node uses epoll, adding more CPU cores automatically lets a single Node process handle more CPU-heavy requests in parallel.
options: True
False
os-concurrency:5.explanation: False. epoll helps waiting, not computing. A single Node process runs JS on one thread; to use more cores you need the cluster module, multiple processes behind a load balancer, or worker_threads.

os-concurrency:6.prompt: In a typical runtime, what is stored on a thread's call stack?
options: All objects created with new, until the function returns
Call frames: return addresses, params, locals
The program's global variables
Memory-mapped files
os-concurrency:6.explanation: The stack holds frames for active calls and is freed automatically on return. Objects whose lifetime isn't tied to a call live on the heap, managed by a garbage collector or by manual free.

options: Memory stored on SSDs and used when RAM is full
Per-process address spaces mapped to physical frames
RAM that is faster than the CPU cache
A heap that only Node.js and the JVM use for garbage collection
os-concurrency:6.explanation: Each process sees a private, contiguous address space; page tables map virtual pages to physical frames (or to disk). This gives isolation and lets the OS overcommit and share pages. It's an OS and hardware feature, not a disk type.

os-concurrency:6.prompt: A program touches a page that is valid but not currently in RAM, so the OS must read it from swap. What is this called?
options: Segmentation fault
Major page fault
Minor page fault
Cache hit
os-concurrency:6.explanation: A major (hard) fault needs disk I/O and costs milliseconds. A minor fault resolves without disk (e.g. the page is already in memory but not yet mapped). A segfault is an invalid access.

os-concurrency:6.prompt: A Linux host is so short of RAM that processes spend most of their time paging to and from disk, and throughput collapses. What is this called?
options: Fragmentation
Thrashing
Deadlock
Preemption
os-concurrency:6.explanation: Thrashing happens when the combined working sets exceed physical memory, so pages are evicted and immediately needed again. Fragmentation is about unusable gaps in free memory, not constant paging.

os-concurrency:6.prompt: Why does the TLB matter for performance?
options: It stores the program's compiled code
It caches address translations to skip page walks
It is where the heap lives
It decides which thread runs next on each core after an interrupt
os-concurrency:6.explanation: Without the TLB, every access would need a multi-level page-table walk. TLB misses are expensive, which is why huge pages (2 MB) help large-memory workloads: one entry covers far more memory.

os-concurrency:6.prompt: A Node container's RSS keeps growing to 1.5 GB while process.memoryUsage().heapUsed stays near 200 MB. Where should you look first?
options: A leak of plain JS objects held in a global array
Off-heap memory: Buffers, native addons, fragmentation
The call stack being too deep
The TLB being too small
os-concurrency:6.explanation: heapUsed only counts V8's JS heap. RSS also includes external memory (Buffers), native allocations and fragmentation, so check memoryUsage().external and arrayBuffers. A JS object leak would show up in heapUsed.

os-concurrency:6.prompt: A Node process in a container with a 512 MB memory limit gets killed with exit code 137 and no JavaScript error. What most likely happened?
options: V8 threw RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
The cgroup OOM killer sent SIGKILL
The event loop deadlocked
An unhandled promise rejection crashed the process with that exit code
os-concurrency:6.explanation: 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL). The cgroup OOM killer can't be caught, so no JS error appears. Set --max-old-space-size below the limit to leave headroom for non-heap memory, so V8 collects or fails visibly first.

distractors: false Maximum call stack size exceeded
os-concurrency:6.explanation: Unbounded recursion exhausts the fixed-size call stack, and V8 throws a catchable RangeError 'Maximum call stack size exceeded' ("too much recursion" is Firefox's wording). Heap exhaustion is different: it usually crashes the process.

os-concurrency:6.prompt: Which statements about stack vs heap are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Each thread has its own stack; threads in a process share the heap
Stack allocation is typically just moving a pointer, so it's very cheap
Objects on the heap are freed automatically when the function that created them returns
Deep recursion can overflow the stack even when plenty of heap is free
The stack can grow without any limit
os-concurrency:6.explanation: Stacks are per-thread, fast and size-limited; heaps are shared and need GC or manual freeing. Heap objects outlive their creating function if referenced, and stacks have fixed or capped sizes.

os-concurrency:6.prompt: What does paging with virtual memory enable? Select all that apply.
options: Isolation: one process can't read another's memory by address
Sharing read-only code pages of a library between processes
Copy-on-write after fork(), so pages are only copied when written
Guaranteed zero page faults
Programs using more virtual memory than physical RAM, backed by swap or lazy allocation
os-concurrency:6.explanation: Per-process page tables give isolation, shared mappings, copy-on-write and overcommit. Page faults are the mechanism that makes lazy allocation and swapping work, so they're expected, not eliminated.

os-concurrency:6.prompt: On Linux, calling malloc for 1 GB usually returns quickly even on a machine with less free RAM, because physical pages are only allocated when they are first touched.
options: True
False
os-concurrency:6.explanation: True. With the default overcommit setting, the kernel reserves address space and assigns physical frames lazily on first write (via page faults). The risk is that the OOM killer may fire later, when the memory is actually used.
